articles.title: Articles and Genders
articles.rule: German has three grammatical genders: masculine (der), feminine (die), and neuter (das). Plural nouns always use 'die' in the nominative.
articles.accusativeRule: In the accusative case, only masculine articles change: 'der' becomes 'den', 'ein' becomes 'einen'.
articles.dativeRule: In the dative case: 'der'/'das' become 'dem', 'die' becomes 'der', and plural 'die' becomes 'den' (+n).

verbs.v2Rule: In a German main clause, the conjugated finite verb is strictly placed in position 2 (V2 rule).
verbs.verbEndRule: In subordinate clauses (introduced by weil, dass, wenn, ob, etc.), the conjugated verb moves to the very end.

cases.nominativ: Subject of the sentence or predicate noun following 'sein' / 'werden'.
cases.akkusativ: Direct object or following accusative prepositions (durch, für, gegen, ohne, um).
cases.dativ: Indirect object (beneficiary) or following dative prepositions (aus, bei, mit, nach, seit, von, zu).
cases.genitiv: Possession or following genitive prepositions (während, wegen, trotz, anstatt).

exercises.gram-1: In Nominative case, 'Tisch' is masculine, requiring 'der'.
exercises.gram-2: Masculine direct object of 'haben' takes the Accusative case, transforming 'ein' into 'einen'.
exercises.gram-3: In Nominative case, 'Katze' is feminine, requiring 'die'.
